desc:
A subsequence of nums is what remains after deleting any number of elements (possibly none) while keeping the order of the others.

Return the length of the longest subsequence of nums that is non-decreasing, that is, every element is greater than or equal to the one before it. For nums = [4, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1] the answer is 4 (the subsequence 1, 2, 2, 3).
hints: Let best[i] be the length of the longest non-decreasing subsequence that ends exactly at index i. How does best[i] depend on the earlier indices?
best[i] = 1 + the largest best[j] over all j < i with nums[j] ≤ nums[i] (or just 1 if there is no such j). The answer is the maximum over all i. That is O(n<sup>2</sup>), good enough here.

For O(n log n), keep a sorted list tails where tails[L-1] is the smallest possible last value of a non-decreasing subsequence of length L. For each x, find the first tail strictly greater than x and overwrite it (or append x if none).
editorial: The straightforward DP defines best[i] as the longest non-decreasing subsequence ending at index i. It is 1 plus the best value among earlier indices j with nums[j] ≤ nums[i]. Two nested loops give O(n2) time and O(n) space.

The faster method keeps tails, where tails[L-1] is the smallest last value over all non-decreasing subsequences of length L seen so far. This list is always sorted. For a new value x, binary-search the first tail that is strictly greater than x (bisect_right) and replace it with x; if no tail is greater, x extends the longest subsequence, so append it. The final length of tails is the answer.

The only difference from the strictly increasing version is the choice of binary search: bisect_right lets equal values stack up, while bisect_left would make them replace each other. Total cost is O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
